terms.definition: The pratyagātmā — the inmost Self that cannot be objectified — is the subject matter (viṣaya) of brahmavidyā.
terms.context: Swamiji explains that brahmavidyā is not knowledge of some external Brahman but of oneself as Brahman. Because brahmavidyā removes the false notion 'I am a body or mind,' its subject matter must be the very Self which underlies all such notions. Śaṅkara quotes Bṛh. Up. 1.4.10 — 'tadātmānamevāved ahaṃ brahmāsmīti' — to show that once one knows the Self thus, one becomes everything, since there is no second reality.

terms.definition: 'These three — name, form, and function — constitute everything that is.' (Bṛh. Up. 1.6.1)
terms.context: Swamiji uses this as the Upaniṣad's own summary of the manifest world. Whatever can be objectified has a name (nāma), a form (rūpa), and a function or action (karma). Brahman alone is beyond all three — it is sarvakāraṇam with no nāma-rūpa of its own. The Bhāṣya cites this verse to signal that the entire domain of avidyā has been covered by the first chapter.

terms.definition: Completely free of all distinguishing characteristics; devoid of every qualification.
terms.context: In the Bhāṣya summary of the second chapter, Śaṅkara says that Brahman — taught through neti-neti — is ekam, advayam, and sarvaviśeṣaśūnyam. Swamiji explains viśeṣa as any mark or attribute that distinguishes one thing from another. Since Brahman has no attributes that set it apart from anything, it cannot be grasped as an object. terms.definition: 'Action is not the cause of liberation, just as fire is not the remedy for heat.' (Sureśvarācārya, BV verse 55)

terms.context: Swamiji's point: everything you think will please you will one day make you sad, and everything thought to hold pleasure does not. Since you love yourself unconditionally, give up all means-born (sādhanodbhūta) happiness without remainder and seek the absolute (ātyantika) happiness — tan niḥśeṣaṃ parityajya sukhamātyantikaṃ śrayet.

terms.definition: Just as in a garland the stick and the rest appear solely through the cognition of the garland, so wife, son and the like arise from ignorance of the inner self.
terms.context: Swamiji ties this to error — seeing a snake where there is a rope, water where there is none. The sraja-daṇḍa (garland-on-a-stick) image shows that pati-jāyā-sutādi are pratyag-ajñāna-hetuja — produced by not knowing the pratyak (inner self); the dearness projected onto them is rooted in that single error.
terms.breakdown_deva: स्रजि दण्ड-आदयः यद्वत् स्रज्-ज्ञान-एक-हेतुकाः — "as in a garland the stick etc. depend solely on cognition of the garland"

terms.definition: That by relation to which even the non-dear becomes dear (and the dear turns non-dear by association) — namely, the self.
terms.context: Swamiji notes that anything becomes dear or hateful only when it is connected or related to you in your perception. A stranger walking on the street is neither a cause of joy nor of sorrow; what attracts or bothers you is invariably bound up with what you take to be yourself.

terms.definition: One freed from all attachment, having liberation alone as his purpose — the description of the seeker qualified (adhikārī) for self-knowledge.
terms.context: Swamiji glosses āsaṅga as ā (extra) + saṅga — excessive value placed on things other than oneself. Having become free of all such interests and having mokṣa as the sole aim, such a one — and not the rāgavān (the man of attachment) — is qualified (adhikriyate) for the rise of pratyag-jñāna.
